title: Kubernetes Fundamentals
description: The core building blocks of Kubernetes — pods, Deployments, and Services — plus how configuration and secrets are externalized, how storage outlives ephemeral containers, how self-healing and autoscaling keep workloads running, and how Helm packages all of it for reuse across environments.

lessons.title: Pods, Deployments, and Services
lessons.description: The three core Kubernetes building blocks: the pod as the smallest deployable unit, the Deployment that declares and reconciles desired state, and the Service that gives a stable way to reach a constantly changing set of pods.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson you should be able to explain what a **pod** is and why it's the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes rather than a container, describe how a **Deployment** keeps a declared number of pod replicas running, and explain how a **Service** gives a stable network identity to a set of pods that are constantly being created and destroyed.

sections.title: 🫘 Pods: the smallest deployable unit
sections.content:
A **pod** is the smallest thing Kubernetes schedules and runs — not a container. A pod wraps one or more containers that:

- Share the same network namespace (same IP address, same port space)
- Can share storage volumes
- Are always scheduled together on the same node
- Live and die together

Most pods run exactly one container. The multi-container case is for tightly coupled helpers — a **sidecar** that ships logs, or a proxy that handles TLS for the main container — not for grouping unrelated services. If two containers don't need to share a network namespace and a lifecycle, they belong in separate pods.

Pods are **ephemeral and disposable**. Kubernetes does not try to keep a specific pod alive forever — if a pod dies, it is gone, and a new pod with a new identity and a new IP address takes its place. You almost never create bare pods directly in production; you create a Deployment, and the Deployment creates and manages pods for you.

sections.title: 📈 Deployments: declaring the desired state
sections.content:
A **Deployment** is a declaration of *desired state*: "I want 3 replicas of this pod template running, always." You don't tell Kubernetes how to get there — you describe the end state and a **controller** continuously reconciles the actual state toward it.

If a pod crashes, the Deployment's controller notices the replica count has dropped below 3 and creates a replacement. If a node dies taking two pods with it, the controller reschedules them elsewhere. If you edit the Deployment to ask for 5 replicas instead of 3, the controller creates 2 more. This reconciliation loop runs continuously, not just at creation time — it's what makes Kubernetes **self-healing**.

A Deployment also manages **rollouts**. When you update the pod template (a new container image, typically), the Deployment replaces old pods with new ones gradually, by default keeping the service available throughout — this is a **rolling update**. If the new version is broken, you can roll back to the previous Deployment revision.

sections.title: 🌐 Services: a stable way to reach a set of pods
sections.content:
Pods are disposable and get new IP addresses every time they're recreated, which is a problem: how does anything reliably talk to "the pods running my API" when those pods' addresses keep changing?

A **Service** solves this by giving a stable virtual IP address and DNS name to a *set* of pods, selected by matching labels (for example, all pods labeled `app: api`). Traffic sent to the Service is load-balanced across whichever pods currently match the label selector — Kubernetes keeps this mapping updated automatically as pods come and go.

The common Service types are:

- **ClusterIP** (default): reachable only from inside the cluster — for internal service-to-service traffic
- **NodePort**: also exposes the Service on a static port on every node — a basic way to reach it from outside
- **LoadBalancer**: asks the cloud provider to provision an external load balancer pointing at the Service

Because Deployments and Services are decoupled — a Service just watches for pods matching a label — you can roll out entirely new pods under a Deployment and client traffic keeps flowing to "the current set of healthy pods" without any reconfiguration.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Creating bare pods instead of a Deployment.** A bare pod has no controller watching it — if it dies, nothing recreates it, and you lose self-healing and rolling updates entirely. Deployments should be the default; bare pods are for debugging or one-off jobs only.

**Forgetting that a Service selects by label, not by name.** If you rename or relabel pods without updating the Service's selector (or vice versa), the Service silently stops routing to anything, or starts routing to the wrong pods — with no error, just traffic going nowhere or somewhere unintended.

**Treating a pod's IP address as stable.** Code or configuration that hardcodes a pod's IP will break the moment that pod is recreated. Always address pods through a Service's stable DNS name, never through an individual pod's address.

questions.question: According to the lesson, why is a pod — not a container — the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?
options: Because containers cannot run without a pod wrapping them under any circumstances
Because a pod groups one or more containers that share a network namespace, can share storage, and are always scheduled and lifecycle-managed together
Because Kubernetes only supports a single container runtime, so pods exist purely for naming purposes
Because pods are a deprecated concept being replaced by containers directly
questions.explanation: The lesson explains a pod wraps containers that share network namespace and storage and are scheduled and destroyed together — that shared unit, not the individual container, is what Kubernetes schedules.

questions.question: Per the "📈 Deployments" section, what does a Deployment actually declare?
options: The exact sequence of shell commands to run to create pods
A desired state — such as "3 replicas of this pod template running" — that a controller continuously reconciles the actual state toward
A one-time snapshot of pods that Kubernetes creates once and never touches again
A list of specific node hostnames pods must run on
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit: you describe desired state and a controller reconciles actual state toward it continuously — that reconciliation loop is what makes Deployments self-healing.

questions.question: In the code example, what does `Service.route()` actually do?
options: It stores a fixed list of pod IDs when the Service is created and never updates it
It recomputes the list of matching pod IDs by filtering whatever pods are passed in against the Service's stored label selector
It deletes any pod that doesn't match its selector
It creates new pods directly, bypassing the Deployment
questions.explanation: `route()` filters `all_pods` by `p.labels == self.selector_labels` every call — it doesn't cache a pod list, so it always reflects whichever pods currently match at call time.

questions.question: In the code example, after `pod-2` is marked unhealthy and `reconcile()` runs, what happens to the pod count and why?
options: It stays at 2 permanently because Kubernetes doesn't replace failed pods automatically
It drops to 2 and stays there until a human manually creates a new pod
`reconcile()` filters out the unhealthy pod and then creates new pods until the count is back to `desired_replicas` (3), so a new pod (e.g. `pod-4`) is added
It grows unbounded because `reconcile()` keeps appending pods every time it's called
questions.explanation: `reconcile()` first drops unhealthy pods (removing `pod-2`), then loops `while len(self.pods) < self.desired_replicas` — with `desired_replicas=3` and 2 pods left, it adds exactly one new pod, bringing the count back to 3.

questions.question: In the code example, after reconciliation replaces `pod-2` with a new pod, does `service.route(deployment.pods)` need to be told about the change?
options: Yes, `Service` must be manually updated with the new pod ID list
No — because `route()` matches on `self.labels` (shared by every pod the Deployment creates), the new pod is included automatically the next time `route()` is called
No, but only because the new pod happens to reuse `pod-2`'s exact ID
Yes, a new `Service` object must be constructed after every reconciliation
questions.explanation: Every pod the Deployment creates — including the replacement — is constructed with the same `api_labels`, so `route()`'s label-matching filter picks it up automatically with no manual update.

questions.question: Which Service type is the default, and where is it reachable from?
options: LoadBalancer; reachable from the public internet by default
NodePort; reachable only from a single specific node
ClusterIP; reachable only from inside the cluster
ExternalName; reachable only from the cloud provider's control plane
questions.explanation: The lesson lists ClusterIP as the default, and it's scoped to internal, in-cluster traffic — NodePort and LoadBalancer are the options for exposing a Service externally.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against creating bare pods directly instead of using a Deployment?
options: Because bare pods use more CPU than pods created by a Deployment
Because a bare pod has no controller watching it, so if it dies nothing recreates it — losing both self-healing and rolling updates
Because Kubernetes technically forbids bare pods from being created at all
Because bare pods cannot be given labels
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section is explicit that a bare pod has no controller, so its death is permanent until a human intervenes — Deployments should be the default precisely to avoid this.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against hardcoding a pod's IP address in code or configuration?
options: Because pod IP addresses are encrypted and cannot be read by application code
Because a pod's IP is not stable — the pod can be recreated at any time with a new IP, so code should address pods through a Service's stable DNS name instead
Because IP addresses are more expensive to route than DNS names
Because Kubernetes pods do not have IP addresses
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly warns that pod IPs are not stable across recreation, and the fix is to always go through a Service's stable identity rather than an individual pod's address.

lessons.title: ConfigMaps, Secrets, and Volumes
lessons.description: How Kubernetes separates configuration from images with ConfigMaps, handles sensitive values with the structurally similar but access-controlled Secrets, and gives pods storage — from ephemeral scratch space to durable PersistentVolumes — that can outlive a container or even the pod itself.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson you should be able to explain why configuration is kept out of a container image using **ConfigMaps**, why sensitive values get the separate **Secrets** mechanism instead, and how **Volumes** give pods storage that survives beyond a single container's lifetime.

sections.title: ⚙️ ConfigMaps: externalized, non-sensitive configuration
sections.content:
A **ConfigMap** holds configuration data — feature flags, URLs, non-sensitive settings — as key-value pairs, kept separate from the container image. This separation matters because it means the *same* image can run in staging with one configuration and in production with another, without rebuilding anything. You mount a ConfigMap into a pod either as environment variables or as files in the container's filesystem.

Because a ConfigMap is a Kubernetes object independent of any specific pod, updating it can push new configuration to every pod that references it (behavior depends on how it's mounted) without a new image build or a full redeploy.

sections.title: 🔐 Secrets: the sensitive counterpart
sections.content:
A **Secret** is structurally almost identical to a ConfigMap — same key-value shape, same mounting mechanisms — but it exists as a separate object type because sensitive data (API keys, database passwords, TLS certificates) needs different handling: tighter access control (RBAC can restrict who can read Secrets specifically), and storage that a cluster can be configured to encrypt at rest.

By default, Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-**encoded**, not encrypted — encoding is not confidentiality, it's just a text-safe representation. Real protection requires enabling encryption-at-rest at the cluster level and restricting who can `get` Secret objects via RBAC. Treating the Secret/ConfigMap split as "automatically secure" is a common and dangerous misunderstanding.

sections.title: 💾 Volumes: storage that outlives a single pod
sections.content:
By default, anything a container writes to its own filesystem disappears when the container restarts — container filesystems are ephemeral. A **Volume** is storage attached to a pod that can outlive individual container restarts within that pod, and — depending on the volume type — can outlive the pod itself.

Common volume types include `emptyDir` (scratch space tied to the pod's lifetime, wiped when the pod is deleted), `configMap`/`secret` volumes (mounting configuration or secret data as files), and **PersistentVolumes** backed by real durable storage (a cloud disk, a network filesystem) that survives even after the pod is deleted. Choosing the right volume type is choosing how long you need the data to live.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming Secrets are encrypted just because they're not ConfigMaps.** By default, Secrets are only base64-encoded, which anyone with read access can trivially decode. Real confidentiality requires enabling encryption-at-rest and locking down RBAC — the Secret/ConfigMap split alone provides organization, not protection.

**Putting data that must survive pod deletion into an `emptyDir` volume.** `emptyDir` is scoped to the pod's lifetime — the moment the pod is deleted, that data is gone. Anything that needs to outlive the pod belongs on a PersistentVolume.

**Baking environment-specific configuration into the container image.** This forces a rebuild for every environment change and defeats the entire purpose of ConfigMaps — configuration should be injected at runtime, not compiled into the image.

questions.question: According to the lesson, why does externalizing configuration into a ConfigMap matter?
options: It makes containers start up faster
The same container image can run in different environments with different configuration, without rebuilding the image
It automatically encrypts all configuration values
It removes the need for environment variables entirely
questions.explanation: The lesson's core point about ConfigMaps is that separating config from the image lets one image run in staging vs. production with different settings, with no rebuild required.

questions.question: Per the "🔐 Secrets" section, what is a Secret's default level of protection?
options: Fully encrypted at rest and in transit automatically, with no configuration needed
Only base64-encoded by default — not encrypted — so real protection needs encryption-at-rest plus RBAC restrictions
Identical to a ConfigMap in every respect, including access control
Stored only in memory and never written to disk under any configuration
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that default Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted, and that real protection requires explicitly enabling cluster-level encryption-at-rest and restricting access via RBAC.

questions.question: In the code example, why does `pod.read_config("log_level")` return `"debug"` after `app_config.data["log_level"] = "debug"` runs?
options: Because `read_config` re-reads a file from disk
Because `pod.config_map` holds a reference to the same `ConfigMap` object, so mutating `app_config.data` is visible immediately through that shared reference
Because Pod automatically polls the ConfigMap every second
It doesn't — the value returned is still `"info"`
questions.explanation: `self.config_map = config_map` stores a reference, not a copy, so any mutation to `app_config.data` is visible the next time `read_config` reads `self.config_map.data`.

questions.question: In the code example, what is `pod.empty_dir` after `pod.delete()` is called?
options: `{"temp_cache_key": "abc123"}`, unchanged
An empty dict `{}`
`None`
It raises an exception
questions.explanation: `delete()` explicitly sets `self.empty_dir = None`, modeling how `emptyDir` volumes are wiped when the pod they belong to is deleted.

questions.question: What does the code example demonstrate about the difference between the ConfigMap reference and the emptyDir volume?
options: Both are wiped at the same time, on pod deletion
The ConfigMap reference reflects live updates from outside the pod, while the emptyDir volume's contents are scoped to (and destroyed with) the pod itself
The ConfigMap is scoped to the pod's lifetime, while emptyDir survives pod deletion
Neither is affected by pod deletion
questions.explanation: The ConfigMap update (`log_level`) shows up live because it's an external, shared object; the emptyDir scratch data disappears specifically because `pod.delete()` clears it — opposite lifetimes.

questions.question: Which volume type is described as surviving even after the pod itself is deleted?
options: `emptyDir`
A `configMap` volume mounted as files
A PersistentVolume backed by durable storage such as a cloud disk or network filesystem
None — all volume types are deleted with the pod
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes `emptyDir` (tied to pod lifetime) from PersistentVolumes, which are explicitly described as surviving even after the pod that used them is deleted.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against assuming Secrets are automatically encrypted just because they're a separate object type from ConfigMaps?
options: Because Secrets are actually less secure than ConfigMaps by design
Because base64 encoding — the default state of a Secret's data — is trivially reversible and provides no real confidentiality without additional cluster configuration
Because Secrets cannot be mounted into pods at all
Because ConfigMaps are always encrypted while Secrets never can be
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section calls out this exact misconception: base64 is an encoding, not encryption, and anyone with read access can trivially decode it without enabling encryption-at-rest and RBAC.

questions.question: Why does the lesson recommend against baking environment-specific configuration into the container image?
options: Because it makes the image too large to store
Because it forces a rebuild of the image for every environment-specific change, defeating the purpose of externalized configuration
Because Kubernetes refuses to run images with embedded configuration
Because it violates container registry naming rules
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section states this directly: baked-in config forces a rebuild per environment change and undermines the whole point of using ConfigMaps to inject config at runtime.

lessons.title: Scaling and Self-Healing
lessons.description: How Kubernetes's reconciliation loop produces automatic self-healing, how Horizontal Pod Autoscaling adjusts replica counts based on metrics, and why the default CPU-based approach breaks down for GPU-bound AI/ML workloads specifically.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson you should be able to explain how Kubernetes self-healing recovers from pod and node failures automatically, how **Horizontal Pod Autoscaling** adjusts replica counts based on load, and why autoscaling has specific limits that matter for AI/ML workloads in particular.

sections.title: 💊 Self-healing in practice
sections.content:
Self-healing isn't a separate feature you turn on — it falls directly out of the reconciliation loop described earlier: a Deployment continuously compares actual pod count against desired replica count and creates replacements whenever they diverge. This covers several failure modes automatically:

- A container crashes → the kubelet on that node restarts it
- A pod fails **readiness/liveness probes** repeatedly → it's killed and replaced
- An entire node goes offline → its pods are rescheduled onto healthy nodes

None of this requires a human to notice and intervene — the cluster is continuously working to close the gap between what's declared and what's actually running.

sections.title: 📈 Horizontal Pod Autoscaling
sections.content:
**Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA)** adjusts a Deployment's replica count automatically based on observed metrics — most commonly CPU utilization, but also memory or custom metrics like requests per second. You declare a target ("keep average CPU utilization near 60%") and a min/max replica range, and the HPA controller periodically checks current utilization and scales replicas up or down to move toward that target.

This is *horizontal* scaling — adding or removing replicas — as opposed to *vertical* scaling, which would mean giving an individual pod more CPU or memory. Horizontal scaling is generally preferred for stateless services because it also improves resilience: more replicas means more redundancy against any single pod or node failing.

sections.title: ⚠️ Autoscaling's limits for AI workloads
sections.content:
HPA's assumptions fit typical web services well, but AI/ML workloads break some of them:

- **GPU scarcity**: scaling up a CPU-bound service just requests more of an abundant resource; scaling up a GPU-bound service may simply fail if no GPU capacity is available in the cluster or region
- **Slow scale-up latency**: a new pod needing a large model loaded into GPU memory can take minutes to become ready, unlike a lightweight web server that's ready in seconds — by the time it's up, the load spike may have passed
- **CPU utilization is a poor proxy for GPU workloads**: a pod running inference can have low CPU usage while its GPU is saturated, so default CPU-based HPA metrics can fail to trigger scaling when it's actually needed

For GPU-bound workloads, scaling decisions typically need custom metrics (GPU utilization, queue depth, request latency) rather than the default CPU metric, and scale-up needs to be triggered earlier to absorb the longer time-to-ready.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Here's a simplified simulation contrasting HPA scaling a CPU-bound service against a GPU-bound service where CPU utilization stays misleadingly low:

```python
def hpa_decide_replicas(current_replicas, current_utilization_pct, target_pct, max_replicas):
    # simplified proportional scaling, matching the real HPA formula's shape
    desired = current_replicas * (current_utilization_pct / target_pct)
    desired = max(1, min(max_replicas, round(desired)))
    return desired

# CPU-bound web service: CPU usage tracks load directly
web_replicas = hpa_decide_replicas(
    current_replicas=4, current_utilization_pct=90, target_pct=60, max_replicas=10
)
print("web service scales to:", web_replicas)  # scales up, CPU signal is meaningful

# GPU-bound inference service: GPU is saturated but CPU usage is low
gpu_cpu_utilization_pct = 20  # misleadingly low, even though the GPU is maxed out
gpu_replicas_using_cpu_metric = hpa_decide_replicas(
    current_replicas=4, current_utilization_pct=gpu_cpu_utilization_pct, target_pct=60, max_replicas=10
)
print("GPU service scales to (CPU metric):", gpu_replicas_using_cpu_metric)  # scales DOWN, wrongly

gpu_utilization_pct = 95  # the metric that actually reflects load
gpu_replicas_using_gpu_metric = hpa_decide_replicas(
    current_replicas=4, current_utilization_pct=gpu_utilization_pct, target_pct=60, max_replicas=10
)
print("GPU service scales to (GPU metric):", gpu_replicas_using_gpu_metric)  # scales up, correctly
```

With `current_replicas=4`, `current_utilization_pct=90`, `target_pct=60`: `desired = 4 * (90/60) = 6.0`, so the web service scales to **6**. Using the CPU metric for the GPU service: `4 * (20/60) = 1.33`, rounding to **1** — HPA would actually shrink the deployment while the GPU is maxed out, exactly backwards. Using the GPU metric instead: `4 * (95/60) = 6.33`, rounding to **6** — the scale-up decision the workload actually needs.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Applying default CPU-based HPA to GPU-bound inference services unmodified.** As the code example shows, this can produce exactly the wrong scaling decision — shrinking a deployment whose GPUs are saturated, because CPU usage looks low. GPU-bound services need GPU or queue-depth metrics.

**Not accounting for slow pod startup when setting scaling thresholds.** If a GPU inference pod takes several minutes to load a model and become ready, waiting until utilization is already critical to trigger scale-up means the new capacity arrives too late to help with that spike.

**Assuming autoscaling can always add capacity.** Horizontal scaling for GPU workloads can hit a hard ceiling — the cluster or region simply may not have more GPU capacity available — unlike CPU/memory scaling, which is rarely capacity-constrained in the same way.

questions.question: Per the "💊 Self-healing" section, does Kubernetes self-healing require a separate feature to be enabled?
options: Yes, it must be explicitly enabled per Deployment
No — it falls directly out of the reconciliation loop that already compares actual vs. desired pod count and creates replacements automatically
Yes, it requires a third-party controller to be installed
No, but it only works for stateless pods
questions.explanation: The lesson states self-healing isn't a separate feature — it's a direct consequence of the same reconciliation loop covered in the pods/Deployments lesson.

questions.question: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling, per the "📈 Horizontal Pod Autoscaling" section?
options: Horizontal scaling adds/removes replicas; vertical scaling gives an individual pod more CPU or memory
Horizontal scaling only applies to databases; vertical scaling only applies to web servers
They are two names for the exact same mechanism
Horizontal scaling changes a pod's resource limits; vertical scaling changes replica count
questions.explanation: The lesson defines horizontal scaling as adjusting replica count and contrasts it explicitly with vertical scaling, which means giving one pod more resources.

questions.question: In the code example, why does `gpu_replicas_using_cpu_metric` come out to 1 instead of scaling up?
options: Because `hpa_decide_replicas` has a bug that always returns 1 for GPU workloads
Because CPU utilization for the GPU service is only 20%, well below the 60% target, so the proportional formula `4 * (20/60) ≈ 1.33` rounds down to 1 — even though the GPU itself is saturated
Because `max_replicas` was set to 1 for the GPU example
Because GPU services always scale to exactly 1 replica by convention
questions.explanation: `desired = current_replicas * (current_utilization_pct / target_pct) = 4 * (20/60) ≈ 1.33`, which `round()`s to 1 — the CPU metric misrepresents the GPU service's actual load.

questions.question: In the code example, what replica count does the GPU service scale to when using the GPU utilization metric (95%) instead of CPU?
questions.explanation: `desired = 4 * (95/60) ≈ 6.33`, which rounds to 6 — matching the web service's scale-up decision and correctly reflecting that the GPU-bound workload actually needs more capacity.

questions.question: What does the code example demonstrate about using CPU utilization as the scaling metric for a GPU-bound service?
options: It produces the same correct scaling decision as a GPU-based metric would
It can produce a scaling decision that's exactly backwards — shrinking replicas while the GPU is actually saturated
It always causes replicas to increase regardless of actual load
CPU metrics are irrelevant because HPA ignores them for GPU pods automatically
questions.explanation: The CPU-metric calculation yields 1 replica (a decrease from 4) while the GPU is at 95% — the opposite of what the workload needs, illustrating exactly the mismatch the lesson warns about.

questions.question: According to the "⚠️ Autoscaling's limits" section, why can slow scale-up latency be a specific problem for GPU inference pods?
options: Because GPU pods are ready in milliseconds, faster than HPA can react
Because loading a large model into GPU memory can take minutes, so by the time a newly scaled pod is ready, the load spike that triggered scaling may have already passed
Because GPU pods never become ready and must be restarted manually
Because HPA cannot create GPU pods at all
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly contrasts a lightweight web server (ready in seconds) with a GPU pod that can take minutes to load a model, meaning new capacity can arrive too late to help.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn that autoscaling cannot always add capacity for GPU-bound workloads?
options: Because Kubernetes limits every Deployment to a fixed maximum of 10 replicas
Because the cluster or region may simply not have more GPU capacity available, unlike CPU/memory which are rarely constrained the same way
Because GPU pods are not allowed to be scaled by HPA under any circumstances
Because scaling GPU workloads requires manual approval from the cloud provider every time
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section calls out GPU scarcity as a hard ceiling that horizontal scaling can hit — a constraint CPU/memory-based scaling rarely runs into.

questions.question: Why does the lesson recommend against waiting until utilization is already critical before triggering scale-up for GPU workloads?
options: Because triggering scale-up early wastes money regardless of load
Because given the slow startup time of GPU pods, waiting until the last moment means new capacity arrives after the load spike has already passed
Because Kubernetes ignores scale-up requests made under high load
Because early triggers cause pods to be scheduled on the wrong node
questions.explanation: This directly follows from the scale-up latency point: with minutes-long readiness times, triggering scale-up earlier is necessary so new capacity actually arrives while it's still needed.

lessons.title: Helm for Packaging
lessons.description: How Helm solves the repetitive-YAML problem with templated charts and per-environment values files, and how release versioning gives Kubernetes deployments the same safety properties as version-controlled code.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson you should be able to explain the repetitive-YAML problem Helm solves, describe what a Helm **chart** is and how templating and values files work together, and explain how Helm's release versioning enables rollback.

sections.title: 📄 The problem: too much repetitive YAML
sections.content: A realistic application might need a Deployment, a Service, a ConfigMap, a Secret, and an Ingress — each as separate YAML files, and each needing near-identical variants for dev, staging, and production (different replica counts, different resource limits, different hostnames). Hand-maintaining all of these separately means the same structural pattern is copy-pasted repeatedly, and any shared bug fix must be applied everywhere by hand.

sections.title: 📦 Helm: templated packages called charts
sections.content:
**Helm** is a package manager for Kubernetes. A **chart** is a bundle of templated YAML manifests plus a `values.yaml` file supplying the parameters that fill in those templates — replica count, image tag, resource limits, and so on. The same chart can be installed multiple times with different values files to produce a dev deployment, a staging deployment, and a production deployment from one shared template set, rather than three sets of hand-maintained YAML.

Installing a chart with a specific values file produces a **release** — a named, tracked instance of that chart's rendered manifests actually running in the cluster.

sections.title: 🔄 Versioning and rollback
sections.content:
Every time you install or upgrade a release, Helm records that as a new **revision** of the release, keeping a history. If an upgrade introduces a problem, `helm rollback` reverts the release to a previous revision's rendered manifests — restoring the exact configuration that was known to work, without hand-reconstructing what changed.

This turns deployment configuration into something with the same safety properties as version-controlled code: you can see what changed between revisions, and you can revert cleanly when something breaks.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Here's a simplified simulation of a chart template being rendered with different values files, and a release history enabling rollback:

```python
def render_template(template, values):
    rendered = dict(template)
    rendered["replicas"] = values["replicaCount"]
    rendered["image"] = f"{values['image']['repository']}:{values['image']['tag']}"
    return rendered

chart_template = {"kind": "Deployment", "name": "api"}

dev_values = {"replicaCount": 1, "image": {"repository": "api", "tag": "dev"}}
prod_values = {"replicaCount": 5, "image": {"repository": "api", "tag": "v2.3.0"}}

dev_release = render_template(chart_template, dev_values)
prod_release = render_template(chart_template, prod_values)
print("dev:", dev_release)
print("prod:", prod_release)

class ReleaseHistory:
    def __init__(self):
        self.revisions = []

    def upgrade(self, template, values):
        rendered = render_template(template, values)
        self.revisions.append(rendered)
        return len(self.revisions)  # revision number

    def rollback(self, revision_number):
        return self.revisions[revision_number - 1]

history = ReleaseHistory()
history.upgrade(chart_template, {"replicaCount": 3, "image": {"repository": "api", "tag": "v1.0.0"}})
broken_revision = history.upgrade(chart_template, {"replicaCount": 3, "image": {"repository": "api", "tag": "v1.1.0-buggy"}})
print("current (broken):", history.revisions[-1])

restored = history.rollback(1)
print("rolled back to revision 1:", restored)
```

`render_template` is the same function used for both `dev_release` and `prod_release` — only the `values` dict differs, so `dev_release["image"]` is `"api:dev"` with `replicas: 1`, while `prod_release["image"]` is `"api:v2.3.0"` with `replicas: 5`, from one shared template. After the second `upgrade()` call installs the buggy `v1.1.0-buggy` tag as revision 2, `history.rollback(1)` returns exactly the revision 1 manifest — `{"kind": "Deployment", "name": "api", "replicas": 3, "image": "api:v1.0.0"}` — restoring the known-good configuration.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Hand-editing rendered manifests in the cluster instead of updating values and re-releasing.** This creates configuration drift between what the chart's values files describe and what's actually running — the next `helm upgrade` can silently overwrite the hand-edit, or the drift makes rollback unreliable.

**Treating `values.yaml` defaults as safe for every environment.** A chart's default values are often tuned for one environment (frequently the least critical). Deploying to production without an explicit production values file can mean shipping with a dev-sized replica count or resource limit.

**Forgetting that rollback reverts the release's manifests, not any stateful data.** Rolling back a Deployment to a previous image version doesn't undo a database migration that new version applied — rollback and data migrations need to be reasoned about separately.

questions.question: According to the "📄 The problem" section, what specifically makes hand-maintained per-environment YAML painful?
options: YAML files cannot be stored in version control
The same structural pattern (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, etc.) is copy-pasted across near-identical dev/staging/production variants, and shared fixes must be applied everywhere by hand
Kubernetes does not support YAML as a configuration format
Each environment requires a completely different container image
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated problem is the repetition of the same structural pattern across environment variants, and the manual burden of propagating any shared fix across all of them.

questions.question: Per the "📦 Helm" section, what is a chart, and what does installing it produce?
options: A chart is a single YAML file; installing it produces a ConfigMap
A chart is a bundle of templated manifests plus a values file; installing it with a specific values file produces a named, tracked release
A chart is a container image; installing it produces a running pod
A chart is a Kubernetes cluster; installing it produces a new node
questions.explanation: The lesson defines a chart as templated manifests plus values, and describes installation as producing a release — a named, tracked instance of the rendered manifests running in the cluster.

questions.question: In the code example, why do `dev_release` and `prod_release` differ even though both come from `render_template(chart_template, ...)`?
options: Because `render_template` is randomized
Because the same template is rendered with different `values` dicts (`dev_values` vs. `prod_values`), producing different `replicas` and `image` fields
Because `chart_template` itself was modified between the two calls
They don't actually differ — the output is identical
questions.explanation: `render_template` only varies its output based on the `values` argument — `chart_template` is shared and unchanged, so the differing `replicaCount` and `image` in `dev_values`/`prod_values` are the entire source of the difference.

questions.question: In the code example, what does `history.rollback(1)` return after the buggy `v1.1.0-buggy` upgrade is applied as revision 2?
options: The revision 2 (buggy) manifest
An empty dict
The revision 1 manifest — `replicas: 3`, image `api:v1.0.0` — restoring the previously known-good configuration
It raises an IndexError
questions.explanation: `rollback(1)` returns `self.revisions[1 - 1]` = `self.revisions[0]`, which is the first `upgrade()` call's rendered output: replicas 3, image `api:v1.0.0`.

questions.question: What does `ReleaseHistory.upgrade()` return, and what does it represent?
options: The rendered manifest itself, with no version tracking
`len(self.revisions)` after appending — the revision number of the just-applied upgrade
A boolean indicating success or failure
The previous revision's manifest
questions.explanation: `upgrade()` appends the new rendered manifest to `self.revisions` and returns `len(self.revisions)`, which is exactly the 1-indexed revision number that upgrade just created.

questions.question: What does the code example illustrate about reusing one chart template across environments?
options: That a separate template must be hand-written for each environment
That the exact same `render_template` function, given only a different `values` dict, produces environment-appropriate output — avoiding maintaining separate near-duplicate manifest sets
That templates cannot vary replica count between environments
That values files are ignored when rendering a template
questions.explanation: The same `render_template(chart_template, values)` call, varying only `values`, produces both the dev and prod manifests — exactly the reuse Helm charts are meant to provide.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against hand-editing rendered manifests directly in the cluster instead of updating chart values?
options: Because Kubernetes forbids manual edits to running resources
Because it creates configuration drift between the values files and what's actually running, which the next `helm upgrade` can silently overwrite or which can make rollback unreliable
Because hand-edited manifests run faster than templated ones
Because Helm automatically deletes any manually edited resource
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section states this directly: hand-editing creates drift from the source-of-truth values files, risking silent overwrites on the next upgrade and undermining rollback reliability.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn that rollback doesn't undo everything a prior upgrade did?
options: Because rollback only reverts the release's manifests, not stateful side effects like a database migration that a newer version applied
Because rollback is purely cosmetic and doesn't actually change anything in the cluster
Because Helm rollback requires re-entering all values by hand
Because rollback only works for ConfigMaps, never for Deployments
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section explicitly separates manifest rollback from stateful changes like database migrations, which rolling back a Deployment's image version does not automatically reverse.
